title: Formal fallacies
note: A formal fallacy is an invalid argument form, detectable from structure alone. Affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent imitate modus ponens and modus tollens, but 'If P then Q' makes P sufficient for Q, not necessary. In a categorical syllogism the middle term must be distributed at least once, and any term distributed in the conclusion must be distributed in its premise.

read.title: Look-alikes that fail
text: A formal fallacy is an argument whose form is invalid, so you can spot it without knowing anything about the subject. The two most common imitate valid rules. Modus ponens says: if P then Q; P; so Q. Its look-alike, affirming the consequent, says: if P then Q; Q; so P. Suppose that if it rains, the street gets wet. The street is wet. Did it rain? Not necessarily; a street sweeper may have passed.

Modus tollens says: if P then Q; not Q; so not P. Its look-alike, denying the antecedent, says: if P then Q; not P; so not Q. It did not rain, so the street is dry? Again, the sweeper shows the gap. The underlying lesson is that 'If P then Q' makes P sufficient for Q, not necessary for it.

Categorical syllogisms have their own formal fallacies. 'All crooks lie; Al lies; so Al is a crook' commits the undistributed middle: the middle term, 'liars', is never used to say something about every liar, so crooks and Al might occupy different parts of that class.
Remember that a bad argument does not prove its conclusion false. Al might be a crook after all. Concluding that a claim is false just because one argument for it fails is itself a mistake.

q.q: What does the street sweeper show in the reading?
o: That rain is necessary for a wet street
That the street can be wet without rain

q.q: Why is 'All crooks lie; Al lies; so Al is a crook' invalid?
o: Its middle term is never distributed

q.q: If an argument for a claim commits a formal fallacy, then
o: the claim may still be true
